title: Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent
lead: A finished country house contains pipe from manufacturers other than the specified brand. The owner demands replacement behind the walls, while the builder seeks the unpaid balance and offers evidence that the pipe is equivalent.

actors.name: Jacob & Youngs, Inc.
actors.role: Builder seeking the unpaid construction balance.

actors.name: Kent
actors.role: Homeowner demanding compliance with the Reading-pipe specification.

actors.name: The architect and plumbing subcontractor
actors.role: Participants whose inspection and installation conduct affected whether the deviation was innocent.

proceedings: The trial court excluded equivalence evidence and directed a verdict for Kent.
The Appellate Division reversed for a new trial.
The Court of Appeals affirmed and directed judgment absolute for the builder under the appeal stipulation; reargument was later denied.
limits: The account transforms the canonical historical brief without a new opinion audit or current-law certification. Majority and dissent sharply differed on the character and extent of the deviation. The separate reargument order is identified by its own citation and participation; it is not merged into the January vote.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The house is occupied before the pipe discrepancy is discovered
sections.cue: Why would exact correction be expensive?
paragraphs: Jacob & Youngs built Kent’s country residence for more than $77,000. Work ceased in June 1914, and Kent occupied the house, leaving $3,483.46 unpaid. The plumbing specifications called for well-galvanized, lap-welded standard wrought-iron pipe manufactured by Reading.

In March 1915, Kent learned that some pipe came from other manufacturers and complained. The architect ordered replacement. Most plumbing was already enclosed, so replacing the entire system would require substantial demolition of the finished house. The builder declined, sought its final-payment certificate, and sued when the certificate was refused.

Manufacturers’ names were stamped at six- or seven-foot intervals, and even the architect had overlooked the discrepancy. The builder offered evidence that the installed brands equaled Reading pipe in quality, appearance, market value, and cost. The trial court excluded it and directed a verdict for Kent. The Appellate Division ordered a new trial, and Kent appealed.

sections.title: Cardozo separates the builder’s duty from a condition of payment
sections.cue: Why might imperfect work still earn the contract balance?
paragraphs: Judge Cardozo’s majority did not find literal compliance. It regarded the evidence as supporting innocent subcontractor oversight rather than fraud or willful substitution and held that a trivial, innocent omission could be compensated without forfeiting the entire unpaid price. A contractual duty remained distinct from whether every departure defeated the owner’s counterperformance obligation.

Some promises were independent, others necessarily dependent, and others could condition payment when a departure was substantial but remain collateral when it was insignificant. Presumed intention and justice in the particular transaction governed. Construction becomes inseparable from land, making forfeiture more severe than rejection of a returnable chattel. The law hesitated to infer an intention that an innocent minor default cause vastly disproportionate loss.

This was no license to install whatever a builder considered equally good. A dominant or pervasive change defeating contractual purpose could not qualify. Art and personal preference could make a substitution significant beyond utility. Courts had to consider purpose, the desire to be satisfied, the explanation for deviation, and the burden of exact adherence. Doubtful factual inferences belonged to the factfinder; certain ones could be resolved judicially.

Apt and certain language could expressly make every term a condition of recovery, but that allocation was not the question here. Nor did the majority extend leniency to a willful transgressor. Because the offered equivalence evidence could show an unintentional and insignificant deviation within the whole project, excluding it and directing a verdict were errors.

sections.title: The allowance depends on the benefit of tearing out the system
sections.cue: Did the court calculate a final repair award?
paragraphs: Completion or replacement cost ordinarily lets an owner obtain the promised work. But where that cost is grossly and unfairly disproportionate to its benefit, diminution in value supplies the allowance. Demolishing parts of this house could cost greatly while equivalent pipe might produce only nominal or no value difference.

Some exposed pipe might have been replaced cheaply, but Kent demanded replacement from cellar to roof. The builder had not reached proof of a precise allowance because exclusion of substantial-performance evidence stopped that progression. The court did not invent a damage number; it explained why proof directed to diminished value need not be defective and why the remedy should avoid recreating disproportionate forfeiture.

sections.title: McLaughlin sees a departure too serious for the majority’s rule
sections.cue: Which record details drove the dissent?
paragraphs: Judge McLaughlin, joined by Judges Pound and Andrews, viewed the conduct as intentional or grossly negligent to equivalent effect. The first delivery of about 1,000 feet had been checked against the Reading requirement, but later orders requested quantities without specifying manufacturer, and later installations went unchecked.

Of about 900 feet exposed and inspected afterward, only seventy bore the required origin. With roughly 2,000–2,500 feet in the system, the dissent found no more than 1,000 feet shown compliant. Procurement records could have demonstrated more, but the builder did not produce that proof.

The dissent accepted recovery for good-faith performance with minor inadvertent omissions, but found this record outside that category. Kent could choose a manufacturer even for personal preference, and equivalent utility could not replace the bargain. The builder also had not proved compliance cost where replacement was feasible. The dissent would reinstate the trial judgment for Kent.

sections.title: The appeal stipulation produces judgment absolute
sections.cue: What did the later reargument order clarify?
paragraphs: On January 25, 1921, the four-Justice majority affirmed the Appellate Division’s order and directed judgment absolute for the builder under the appeal stipulation, with costs in all courts. Chief Judge Hiscock and Judges Hogan and Crane joined Cardozo. Thus the ultimate disposition was not merely another trial.

On March 8, a separate per curiam order denied reargument. It rejected the contention that the court had overlooked a covenant to replace defective work. For trivial innocent defects, that covenant, like the installation covenant, remained an independent, collateral obligation rather than a condition; the duty survived while the remedy was damages. Hiscock, Cardozo, Pound, McLaughlin, Crane, and Andrews were listed as concurring in that order, a different participation record from the January division.
